paper_title: EmbeddingGemma 2: Unified and Efficient Multimodal Representations

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We present EmbeddingGemma 2, an open multimodal embedding model which natively represents text, images, audio, video, and combinations thereof in a unified space. Our approach introduces improvements such as simplified per-layer embeddings and a multi-stage curriculum with modality and objective progression which ensure strong quality across unimodal, cross-modal, and mixed-modal evaluations. Notably, in comprehensive embedding benchmarks across all modalities, EmbeddingGemma 2 establishes a new Pareto frontier, outperforming both specialist models and models two to twelve times larger. Furthermore, our design offers flexibility for resource-constrained environments, supporting selective modality encoder loading, adjustable vision token budgets, truncatable embedding dimensions, and quantized weights. We present ablations analyzing key decisions and release EmbeddingGemma 2 to promote further research.

Notably, in comprehensive embedding benchmarks across all modalities, EmbeddingGemma 2 establishes new Pareto frontier, outperforming both specialist models and models two to twelve times larger. Furthermore, our design offers flexibility for resource-constrained environments, supporting selective modality encoder loading, adjustable vision token budgets, truncatable embedding dimensions, and quantized weights. We present ablations analyzing key decisions and release EmbeddingGemma 2 to promote further research. 1. Introduction Embedding models map data to fixed-length vector representations, placing semantically similar data near each other in the embedding space. Text embedding models have become popular choice for tasks like information retrieval, semantic similarity, clustering, and retrieval-augmented generation. However, to work with audio and visual data, these require additional tools like automatic speech recognition (ASR) and image captioners which both add computational cost and fail to capture signals like fine-grained visual details and non-verbal or environmental sounds. Multimodal embedding models like CLIP [1], ALIGN [2], and SigLIP [3] add modality tower for vision, and so achieve strong cross-modal quality, but they are unable to natively process mixed-modal input to capture interactions between input modalities. Recent efforts have adapted Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) into embedding models that allow interleaved mixed-modal input and support more complex tasks such as visual question answering and visual grounding [4, 5, 6, 7]; subsequent work has built on more capable MLLMs to incorporate video and audio modalities [8, 9, 10, 11, 12]. However, as MLLMs have grown in size, so have embedding models adapted from them. These models typically contain several billion parameters, making them prohibitively expensive for applications that are latency-sensitive, high-throughput, or require on-device deployment for privacy or offline access. 1See Contributions and Acknowledgements section. Co-first authors; equal contributions. Corresponding author: hschechter@google.com 2026 Google DeepMind. All rights reserved EmbeddingGemma 2: Unified and Efficient Multimodal Representations Figure 1 EmbeddingGemma 2 natively maps text, images, video, audio, and combinations thereof into unified, semantically-aligned vector space. In this paper, we introduce EmbeddingGemma 2,2 744M-parameter general-purpose multimodal embedding model that maps text, images, video, and audioas well as arbitrary interleaved combinations thereofinto single unified embedding space (Figure 1). EmbeddingGemma 2 combines 271M-parameter bidirectional transformer backbone (embedder included) with 167M-parameter vision encoder and 305M-parameter audio encoder. The modality encoders independently convert media into sequences of soft token embeddings that enter the shared transformer backbone, which means these parameters are modular: EmbeddingGemma 2 can alternatively be run with 271M parameters as text-only model, with 439M as vision-language model, or with 577M as an audio-language model. The model builds on the architecture and weights from the capable Gemma 4 model family [13] and learns from the powerful Gemini Embedding 2 model [8]. Our training regime consists of three stages spanning various tasks, modalities, and domains, which results in broadly capable model, excelling at problems like code search, visual question answering, video moment retrieval, audio classification, and much more. We separate text-only and multimodal training as form of curriculum learning, and separate distillation from contrastive and regularization objectives in order to effectively learn an embedding space tailored to the model. For extreme resource-constrained settings, the model offers high-quality truncated embeddings and separate checkpoints adapted with quantization-aware training. We present ablation studies explaining our architectural and training choices. Recipe Initialization EmbeddingGemma 2 builds directly on Gemma 4s extensive world knowledge and capabilities. The backbone is adapted from pretrained Gemma 4 decoder-only model, switching the causal attention mask to bidirectional attention to enable fully contextual token representations [34, 35, 36, 8]. We omit explicit adaptation stages for bidirectional attention [23, 37], which can be costly and have been shown to be unnecessary for learning expressive representations [23, 38]. We also remove the PLE-specific token lookup table (detailed in Section 3.1), and add mean pooling [39, 23], linear projection, and ℓ2-normalization after the transformer. The vision encoder is initialized with the smaller Gemma 4 vision encoder and further trained in the two multimodal stages, which we show in Section 3 to be critical for quality. The audio encoder is bit-identical to that in the Gemma 4 E2B and E4B models [13] and kept frozen during training. We then train EmbeddingGemma 2 on mixture of embedding tasks spanning various modalities and task types. In total, the model sees approximately 2.9T tokens, of which 300B are seen during text pre-finetuning, 2T during multimodal pre-finetuning, and 600B during multimodal finetuning. Text Pre-finetuning We begin with pre-finetuning stage like the one in Schechter Vera et al. [23]. This entails large-scale unsupervised data mixture of query-target pairs from question answering, sentence similarity, code retrieval, and web search tasks using various languages. As before, we opt for larger batch size both to stabilize the gradient and to provide more (in-batch) negatives for each input example. In this stage we almost exclusively employ distillation loss, with only an additional contrastive loss using small weight. Here, as with subsequent stages, tasks are sampled at pre-determined, empirically defined rates. We found the inclusion of text-only stage important for the models final text quality. This stage can be seen as form of curriculum learning, or as an implicit warm-up for the bidirectional attention, similar to BehnamGhader et al. [37]; it has also been shown to enhance the discriminability of both text and non-text embeddings [10]. Multimodal Pre-finetuning We then continue with pre-finetuning, but with new mixture which also includes inputs with images, audio, video, and documents across unimodal, cross-modal, and mixed-modal tasks, most with additional hard negatives. The text tasks in this stage and the next include those described in the finetuning stage of Schechter Vera et al. [23], which aim to cover task diversity, language diversity, and coding capability. In this stage, we exclusively employ distillation loss, to inherit the teachers ability to map diverse and mixed modalities into shared semantic space. This allows the model to learn tailored embedding space independent of its teacher, as the teachers embedding space is not optimized for the students architecture, size, and MRL subdimensions. We also add other losses which aim to shape the final embedding space to have desirable properties: spread-out regularizer and MRL losses. As in Schechter Vera et al. [23], we transition to smaller learning rates and batch sizes, and shift towards higher-quality, task-specific datasets, such as tool retrieval, audio captioning, video ranking, medical imaging, visual product search, cropped-object retrieval, and academic question-answering. Model Merging Finally, we combine checkpoints from our finetuning run by averaging their weights, to improve our final models quality and robustness. Rather than running multiple finetuning jobs, either with different data mixture rates [23] or with different hyperparameters [40], we merge checkpoints along single finetuning trajectory [41]. Specifically, we compute an unweighted average between the final checkpoint from the finetuning run and significantly earlier checkpoint from the same run. Like Wortsman et al. [42], which similarly merges pretrained and finetuned checkpoints, we found that this helps mitigate degradation on tasks that overfit during finetuning, while also further improving performance on tasks that already benefited from finetuning. Quantization-Aware Training We additionally provide quantized versions of EmbeddingGemma 2 in different quantization configurations. We provide checkpoints with two types of weight representations for the backbone: int4 per-block (Q4_0) and int4 per-channel (Q4_C). For the modality encoders, we follow the quantization schemes used in Gemma 4: the vision encoder uses 8-bit precision for both weights and activations (W8A8), and the audio encoder uses 8-bit activation precision and {2, 4, 8}-bit weight precision varying by layer cluster. We apply quantization-aware training [QAT, 43] to both the backbone and vision encoder to minimize quality degradation (the audio encoder is taken directly from Gemma 4). However, instead of applying QAT directly in the finetuning stage as in Schechter Vera et al. [23], we introduce separate post-merging tail-patch stage in which we distill (and initialize) our QAT checkpoint from the frozen float checkpoint [44]. This allows for more resource-efficient QAT stage and narrows the gap in quality between the float and quantized checkpoints for some evaluations, notably MTEB(English, v2). Ablation Studies We analyze some key design choices to better understand how they contributed to EmbeddingGemma 2s ability to produce high-quality embeddings across modalities, domains, and task types. Baseline and ablation models use an intermediate recipe and so numbers are not representative of the final model. Unless otherwise stated, the experiments run finetuning on pre-finetuned model. We evaluate the models on MMEB-v2 as it covers various tasks involving combinations of text, images, documents, and video, excluding only audio. 3.1. Per-Layer Embeddings Table Gemma 3n and Gemma 4 incorporate Per-Layer Embeddings (PLE) to inject token-level information into intermediate transformer layers. Specifically, they combine learned projection of the main token embedding with an additional dedicated PLE lookup table. However, dedicated PLE lookup table provides no direct signals for non-text modalities and consumes additional memory. We utilize only the projection, as described in detail in Section 2.1; this way, we continue providing per-layer inputs but can omit the lookup table. We compare our approach to PLE with lookup table in Table 2. Removing the dedicated PLE table not only reduces parameter overhead, but also strengthens performance across all three categories (notably +0.69 on Video and +0.61 on VisDoc), confirming that deriving per-layer inputs solely from the shared 𝑑𝑀-dimensional embedding space improves multimodal representation quality. We also found similar improvements in text-only evaluations, where one might expect the lookup table to help the most. 3.2. Finetuning Stage We investigate whether the gains from our finetuning stage are truly driven by difference in recipe or merely by extending training. Starting from the multimodal pre-finetuning checkpoint, we compare running the multimodal finetuning stage against continuing distillation for an approximately computeequivalent duration (the same number of steps, but with larger batch sizes on distillation). Table 3 shows that while distillation plateaus, transitioning to the finetuning recipe with contrastive and spread-out objectives boosts performance significantly for image and video tasks while yielding similar results for visual documents. This demonstrates that the finetuning stage enables the model to move beyond imitating its teacher and learn better-optimized representation space. Vision Encoder Training MLLMs often keep modality encoders frozen throughout training [45, 46, 47, 13]. This strategy is also popular in recent multimodal embedding models [48, 9, 49, 4]. For MLLMs, ablations investigating whether freezing or unfreezing the vision encoder is better are mixed [50, 45, 51]. However, we show in Table 4 that, though the Gemma 4 vision encoder is quite strong by itself, training the vision encoder greatly improves performance of the resulting embeddings on multimodal tasks. Analogous gains are likely possible by further training the audio encoder. Note that both runs here start with text pre-finetuning checkpoint and run multimodal pre-finetuning, to ensure the vision encoder has not already been updated prior to either experiment. Some MLLMs manage to additionally keep the backbone frozen [52]. Hönicke et al. [49] similarly joins backbone text embedding model with modality encoders, keeping each of them frozen. This prevents users from having to backfill embedding databases created with the text embedding model; however, it is possible to translate embeddings from one models space to another [53], even without access to paired data or to the original models [54]. Moreover, freezing text-only backbone empirically seems to limit its ability to understand multimodal inputs, and indeed many of the strongest multimodal embedding models finetune the backbone alongside the modality encoders [12, 10]. 3.4. Vision Token Budgets We train EmbeddingGemma 2 with budget of 280 vision tokens for images and 140 tokens per frame for videos, but the underlying Gemma 4 vision encoder supports budgets from 70 to 1120 tokens. In Table 5 (top), we show the effect of using different vision token budgets at inference time using an intermediate checkpoint trained with 280 tokens per image and 140 per frame. Overall performance scales monotonically, with some distinct modality-specific behaviors. Visual document 10 EmbeddingGemma 2: Unified and Efficient Multimodal Representations tasks are highly sensitive to fine-grained details and continue to improve greatly past the training budget; image quality in aggregate begins to saturate at the 280-token budget (despite continued gains on several individual tasks); and video performance actually degrades between 280 tokens and 560, likely because the excessive sequence lengths dilute attention and mean-pooled representations. Additionally, we compare models trained with 70 vs. 140 per-frame video tokens (Table 5, bottom) to see whether training with smaller vision budget could improve quality when using smaller vision budgets at inference time, for resource-constrained deployment. When evaluated with 70 tokens, training with 70 video tokens improves performance on video tasks, as the model is directly exposed to 70-token frames during training. But this advantage does not hold for image or visual document tasks, which drop in quality. This is likely because a) single-image tasks, which continue to be trained with 280 tokens, are treated as separate modality and do not benefit from seeing 70-token video frames; and b) coarser video representations discard spatial details that otherwise transfer to stronger general visual representations. The latter is further supported when evaluating with 140 tokens, where training with 70 video tokens degrades performance even more, and across modalitiesthis makes the 140-token video budget preferable across both evaluation regimes. More gains are likely possible by increasing train-time budgets, but with seemingly diminishing returns and at significant computational cost. 4. Evaluation We evaluate EmbeddingGemma 2 on comprehensive set of benchmarks across diverse modalities, task types, domains, and languages. Specifically, we report numbers from the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark [MTEB, 55, 56] for natural language and code; the Massive Multimodal Embedding Benchmark v2 [MMEB-v2, 57] and Massive Image Embedding Benchmark [MIEB-lite, 58] for image, video, and visual documents; and the Massive Sound Embedding Benchmark and Massive Audio Embedding Benchmark for speech, music, and environmental sounds [MSEB and MAEB, 59, 60]. We provide summary of our results in Table 6 and dive into each benchmark in more detail below. 4.1. Methods We select as baselines the top-ranked models on each benchmark, including both modality specialists and general-purpose embedding models which support all evaluated modalities. For MTEB, MAEB, and MIEB(lite), we compare against models under 1B parameters; for MMEB-v2, we include models under 2B parameters, as small models are scarce. Because it is one of the most directly comparable models, we evaluate jina-embeddings-v5-omni-nano on MMEB-v2 using its official implementation and verify that, on the subset reported in Hönicke et al. [49], our reproduced score is slightly higher. All other baseline scores are sourced from public leaderboards. We restrict our analysis to single-vector models, given the disparity in storage and latency costs with multi-vector models, and omit models trained on >25% of the evaluation data, as data contamination undermines the evaluations validity. We evaluate EmbeddingGemma 2 using half-precision weights (bfloat16) and the seven types of task instructions detailed in Appendix A. We use different sequence lengths depending on the modality and task type. For visual inputs, we use up to 𝑁frm = 32 frames per video at 140 vision tokens per frame and 280 vision tokens per image to reflect realistic model use, though we note that higher vision token budgets could yield further gains, particularly for visual documents (Section 3.4). Because most baseline models support limited modalities, we count only the parameters EmbeddingGemma 2 utilized for each benchmark; other models parameter counts are as reported on respective leaderboards. On MAEB, EmbeddingGemma 2 again sets new frontier for efficiency. Notably, among sub-1B models, it achieves state-of-the-art scores on any-to-any retrieval and audio classification  (Table 10)  , as well as on about third of all individual tasks. It is also state-of-the-art among models of all sizes for classification of audio pairs and sixth of all individual tasks. Its mean task score is only about 0.2 points away from the best model under 1B parameters, and about 3.5 points away from the highest-scoring model overall. Even its 128-dimensional embeddings beat every other sub-1B model. On average, the model surpasses various audio-text specialists, but there is an interesting specialization divide between them. While EmbeddingGemma 2 does beat specialists like CLAP at non-speech tasks like clustering vehicle sounds (VehicleSoundClustering), these models still outperform in tasks like audio captioning (ClothoT2ARetrieval). In speech tasks, EmbeddingGemma 2 sets the state of the art even in tasks with multiple languages (FleursT2ARetrieval) and singing (JamAltLyricA2TRetrieval). But it sometimes struggles at zero-shot tasks with paralinguistic focus, despite understanding the acoustics deep down. For example, it struggles tremendously at clustering speakers by gender (VoxPopuliGenderClustering: 0.40), but recovers quickly when doing the same task with linear probe (IEMOCAPGender: 66.40). The models excellence on spoken language is further underscored on MSEB. Even when using ASR and text embeddings, EmbeddingGemma 2 greatly outperforms EmbeddingGemma 1, indicating the strength persists throughout modalities  (Table 11)  . Encoding audio natively yields another even larger improvement. Instead of suffering from transcription errors from accents, homophones, or artifacts, native audio inputs preserve these signals and let the model take them into account. As result, even the 256-dimensional embeddings greatly outperform the full-dimension ASR embeddings. 5. Future Work Our work points to several concrete directions for future research. EmbeddingGemma 2 supports long sequences and variable vision token budgets, but further extending context length, for example via content-aware methods, could enable direct indexing of full-length media, improve performance on long-horizon tasks, and support novel agentic memory systems. Innovations such as encoder-free architectures could enable both quality improvements and further reductions in memory footprint and latency. Changes in training paradigms like the introduction of end-to-end RAG training present another opportunity to further optimize embedding models for downstream use. As interleaved all-to-all multimodal search becomes more prevalent, evaluation frameworks that represent novel use cases will become more important. At the same time, EmbeddingGemma 2s utility extends far beyond single-vector retrieval, serving as general-purpose multimodal encoder. Operating on its final embeddings or unpooled token representations, the model can be adapted into (or may even excel zero-shot as) general decision model [61, 62, 63, 64], model router [65], reward model [66], reranker [67], speech-to-text model [68, 69], late interaction retriever [70, 71, 72], and much more. 6. Conclusion EmbeddingGemma 2 builds on its predecessor with smaller, stronger backbone and native multimodal capabilities. Our approach introduces improvements like simplified per-layer embeddings and multistage curriculum with both modality and objective progression. This enables EmbeddingGemma 2 to set new Pareto frontier across text, vision, and audio benchmarks, often surpassing specialist and general-purpose models several times larger. With native support for weight quantization, embedding truncation, and modular encoder loading, EmbeddingGemma 2 makes high-quality multimodal embeddings practical in resource-constrained and on-device settings. We release EmbeddingGemma 2 checkpoints to the community to accelerate research and development, for both off-the-shelf use and as foundational multimodal encoder. 15 EmbeddingGemma 2: Unified and Efficient Multimodal Representations
